Think of your session as **one team**: you (the lead) plus the subagents you

`horizon run` is your team working through its task. Other runs are **other
teams** working in parallel on the *same shared workspace* — one Lean project set,
one roadmap/board, one ledger, one inbox.

You do not manage other teams and they do not manage you. You coordinate through
**shared state**, not meetings:

- **The board (roadmap)** is the shared plan. Keep your items' status/owner/

- **The inbox** is asynchronous messaging + memory across teams (skill:

Before you start, be aware of who else is live (see "Is another run live" below).
A short **synchronizer** digest is printed to stderr at the start of your CLI

other live runs. Read it; it is how you stay aware without asking anyone. A new
conversation or reply invalidates the digest cache immediately. If stderr is

`$ARCHON_HORIZON_ROOT/config.yaml`. Read what you need, when you need it — via the

  \cref{thm:pic0_isAbelianVariety}. For a smooth group scheme over a field the
  relative dimension is constant and equals the dimension of the tangent space at
  the identity, which is \(H^1(C,\mathcal O_C)\) by

  is representable. Then for every \(P\in C(k)\), the scheme \(\Pic^0_{C/k}\)
  satisfies the Albanese universal property for the pointed curve \((C,P)\).
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
  \uses{lem:pic0_isAlbanese_algClosed}
  For \(g(C) > 0\) and \(k\) algebraically closed this is
  \cref{lem:pic0_isAlbanese_algClosed}.

  closed case over \(k^s\) and descend: the universal morphism and the factoring
  homomorphism are unique, so they are Galois-equivariant and descend to \(k\).

3	A Lean 4 formalization of the Jacobian of a smooth, proper, geometrically
4	irreducible curve over a field.  The project takes the Picard-scheme route: build
5	the relative Picard functor, represent it, identify its identity component as an
6	abelian variety of dimension the genus, and derive the Albanese universal

3	description: The LaTeX-subset blueprint format and house style — environments, \uses/\lean/\leanok/\mathlibok/\notready, the math-purity rule, and complete (not sketched) proofs.
4	---
5	
6	Blueprints are a LaTeX subset (the `leanblueprint` dialect) parsed into the DAG.
7	Write timeless mathematics — a standalone document, not a project journal.
8	
9	## Environments
10	
11	Each declaration is an amsthm-style environment; the recognized ones are
12	`theorem`, `lemma`, `proposition`, `corollary`, `definition`, `remark`,
13	`example`, `notation`, `convention`, and `proof`. A statement environment plus
14	its following `proof` environment form one node's content.
15	
16	## Per-node macros
17	
18	- `\label{id}` — a stable id (the DAG node key).
19	- `\lean{Name}` — the Lean declaration(s) this node formalizes; comma-separate to
20	  bind several (`\lean{a, b}`) when they jointly formalize the node's statement.
21	  Each named declaration's signature must match the statement. The mapping need
22	  not be 1-to-1: a node may name several declarations, and Lean may carry
23	  auxiliary declarations with no node at all.
24	- `\uses{a,b}` — dependencies on other nodes' labels; these drive the DAG edges.
25	  Add an edge instead of re-explaining a dependency in prose. Put `\uses` in the
26	  statement for definitional deps and in the `proof` for deps used only in the
27	  proof.
28	- `\source{slug:page-0001}` — reference anchors for UI popups and audit trails.
29	  Use page-level ids from `references/<slug>/tex/page-0001.tex` or an equivalent
30	  manifest entry. Multiple anchors may be comma-separated.
31	- `\leanok` — the Lean is written and checked. Honest only when its Lean is
32	  actually checked *and* its dependencies are too. On a `proof`, it means the
33	  proof is formalized; on a statement, the signature is formalized.
34	- `\mathlibok` — the declaration is already available in mathlib (no
35	  formalization needed; treat as a leaf).
36	
37	## House style
38	
39	- **Pure mathematics only.** No Lean tactics, typeclass/implementation notes, or
40	  semi-Lean pseudocode. No project history ("since iter N", "our failed route")
41	  and no conversational filler. Not every Lean helper needs its own node —
42	  auxiliary or implementation-only declarations can stay unnoded; add a node when
43	  the result is mathematically meaningful in its own right. In particular, never
44	  add a `Formalization note` paragraph to blueprint `.tex`: attach implementation
45	  details, failed approaches, and mechanization caveats to the statement's hgraph
46	  node with `horizon graph ... add comment` instead.
47	- **Complete proofs, not sketches.** A node's `proof` is a real, rigorous
48	  mathematical proof a reader could check — not a hand-wave or a TODO. The way to
49	  keep it short is to *split*, not to abbreviate: if a proof is long or a node
50	  grows past a short paragraph, break out the hard step as its own `\uses`-linked
51	  lemma (down to sentence-sized lemmas if needed) so each node stays small and
52	  its proof stays complete.
53	- **One statement's worth per node.** Keep each node to a single mathematical
54	  statement; don't restate Lean source as prose.
55	- **Cite by source link, not quote comments.** Add `\source{...}` to the
56	  relevant node. Keep the retrieved/transcribed page text in `references/` (for
57	  example `references/<slug>/tex/page-0042.tex`) and let the UI expose it; do not
58	  paste verbatim source quotes into `% QUOTE` comments inside the blueprint.
